title: You are right too
hook: as judge he tells both quarreling men they're right, and when his wife objects, tells her she's right too (Nasruddin tale)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nasruddin rode his donkey backward so he could see his students: face the other way.

Two friends, a couple, two coworkers, a family group chat. An argument breaks out, and both sides turn to whoever is watching: tell them I'm right. Be the judge. Somebody has to win. In the old stories, Nasruddin gets this job for real. For a while, the tales say, he serves as the town's judge, the qadi. Two men walk into his courtroom, red in the face, each sure the other has wronged him. Nasruddin settles into his seat and listens. What he says next is the whole joke.
screen: `TELL THEM I'M RIGHT.` → `NASRUDDIN, THE JUDGE.` → `TWO MEN, RED IN THE FACE.`

segments.voice: The first man tells his side. It's convincing. Nasruddin nods: you're right. The second man jumps in, furious, and tells his side. It's convincing too. Nasruddin nods: you're right. Then his wife, listening from the next room, and in some tellings it's a clerk or a neighbor, can't stand it. They can't both be right! Nasruddin thinks it over and says: you know, you're right too. It's a joke first. Let it be a joke. But look at what it catches. We tend to hear an argument as a contest with one winner, and we pick our winner fast, often before the second person has finished talking. Nasruddin can't. Each time someone speaks, he actually hears them, and finds something true. Quarrels are often like that: each side holds a real piece, a real hurt, a real fact, a real fear. The story cuts the other way too. A judge who agrees with everyone has decided nothing; the men still have their quarrel. Some things do need a decision, and the tale is laughing at Nasruddin as well. So it isn't telling you never to choose. It's asking you to notice how fast you choose, and what you miss when you do. Listen long enough to say, honestly, you're right, about something, to each person. Then decide, if you have to.
screen: `YOU'RE RIGHT. AND YOU'RE RIGHT.` · `WE PICK A WINNER FAST.` · `EACH SIDE HOLDS A REAL PIECE.` · `A JUDGE WHO DECIDES NOTHING.` · then, large: `YOU'RE RIGHT TOO.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a disagreement you're close to, yours or someone else's, and let each person speak in your head. Find one thing each of them is right about; if you're one of the two, find what the other person is right about. Don't decide who wins: hold both, the way Nasruddin does, and breathe.
qadi, the Arabic word for judge. Nasruddin held that role, finding something true in each person who speaks, even the one who says they can't both be right.
Your line: you are also right. The joke is on the judge, too. Day thirty-nine, done.

howItsDone: Nasruddin's judge stories are told across Turkey, Iran and Central Asia, often to children and in classrooms, as a joke about snap judgments; in some tellings the objector is his wife, in others a clerk or a neighbor.

original.note: Arabic, qadi: a judge. In Turkish it became kadı, the title Nasruddin holds in these tales.

trapdoor: what you thought: a silly judge who can't make up his mind.
what it means: most quarrels have a real piece on each side, and we pick a winner before we've heard them.
what a scholar hears: the qadi, the town judge, is a stock role in Nasruddin tales, and the joke works on both the listener and the judge.
